title: Query Hints and Parameter Sniffing
description: Diagnose a stored procedure that is fast for one parameter and slow for another, and fix it properly.

data.text: A stored procedure `sp_GetOrders @Status` runs in 40 ms when called with `'Open'` (500 rows) but takes 12 seconds with `'Closed'` (9 million rows). The plan was compiled on the first call of the day. Explain the cause, and rank your options from best to worst.

data.title: SQL Solution
data.code:
-- 1. Best fix when estimates truly vary wildly: recompile just this statement.
--    Cost is a compile per execution; correctness of the plan is guaranteed.
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE dbo.sp_GetOrders @Status nvarchar(20)
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE Status = @Status
    OPTION (RECOMPILE);
END;
GO

-- 2. Better when only a couple of values are skewed: branch and give each its own plan.
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE dbo.sp_GetOrdersBranched @Status nvarchar(20)
AS
BEGIN
    IF @Status = 'Closed'
        SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM dbo.Orders
        WHERE Status = @Status OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR (@Status = 'Closed'));
    ELSE
        SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM dbo.Orders
        WHERE Status = @Status OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR (@Status = 'Open'));
END;
GO

-- 3. Parameterise properly instead of concatenating: keep the plan reusable.
--    (Never build WHERE clauses by string concatenation — that defeats plan caching
--     entirely and invites SQL injection.)

-- 4. Last resort only: OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN) — stable but usually mediocre.
SELECT OrderId FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = @Status
OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR (@Status UNKNOWN));

data.title: Explanation
data.text: This is **parameter sniffing**: the optimizer compiles the plan using the parameter values of the *first* execution. If that call used `'Open'`, the plan is built for 500 rows (nested loop, nonclustered index seek) and that plan is then reused for `'Closed'`, where it performs millions of lookups. Order of preference: **`OPTION (RECOMPILE)`** on the individual statement when parameter values genuinely produce different optimal plans (small compile cost, correct plan every time); **branching with `OPTIMIZE FOR`** when only one or two values are skewed and the procedure is hot enough that the compile cost matters; **plain parameterisation** (never string-concatenated SQL) so plans stay cacheable; **`OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN`** only when you cannot predict values at all and can accept a consistently average plan. Hints are a scalpel, not a default — reach for `OPTION (FORCE ORDER)` or `INDEX =` hints only after you have fixed statistics and indexing.
